ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are two schematic diagrams in the figure. In Figure I, the left side is labeled wall 2, and the right side is labeled wall 1; block B is located in the middle, connected on the left through spring S2 to support M2, and on the right through spring S1 to support M1. In Figure II, block B is moved toward wall 1, and the displacement x relative to the original equilibrium position is marked in the figure; supports M1 and M2 are drawn as movable black supports rather than fixed on the walls. The problem statement gives that the stiffness coefficient of S1 is k, the stiffness coefficient of S2 is 4k, the masses of the springs and supports are negligible, and there is no friction. Reasoning: According to the problem statement and the diagram, the supports are not fixed on the walls and their masses are negligible, so a free massless support cannot maintain the stretching of a spring by itself to store energy; at an endpoint position, only the spring supported by the wall side stores elastic potential energy. When block B is displaced by x toward wall 1 to the right-side turning point, the support on the S2 side can move along, S2 does not store energy, and only S1 is compressed, with energy E_right = (1/2) k x^2. The block then returns and reaches the maximum displacement y toward wall 2; the S1-side support can move along and does not store energy, and only S2 is compressed, with energy E_left = (1/2)(4k)y^2. With no friction, mechanical energy is conserved, so (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2)(4k)y^2. Simplifying gives x^2 = 4y^2, therefore y/x = 1/2.

raw_record.question_text: A block (B) is attached to two unstretched springs S1 and S2 with spring constants $k$ and $4k$, respectively (see figure I). The other ends are attached to identical supports M1 and M2 not attached to the walls. The springs and supports have negligible mass. There is no friction anywhere. The block B is displaced towards wall 1 by a small distance $x$ (figure II) and released. The block returns and moves a maximum distance $y$ towards wall 2. Displacements $x$ and $y$ are measured with respect to the equilibrium position of the block B. What is the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$?

method.method_draft: First read the diagram: in figure I, block B is between spring S2 on the left, connected to support M2 near wall 2, and spring S1 on the right, connected to support M1 near wall 1. In figure II, B is displaced toward wall 1 by x; because M2 is not fixed to wall 2, the left support has shifted along with the block, so S2 is not stretched, while S1 is compressed against the right support/wall side. From the text, S1 has spring constant k, S2 has spring constant 4k, all other parts are negligible mass, and there is no friction. Use the bridge rule that a free massless support cannot store energy by holding a stretched spring; only the spring braced against a wall at a turning point stores elastic energy. Thus at the right turning point the energy is only in S1: E = (1/2)kx^2. At the left turning point, the right support can follow so S1 is unstretched, while S2 is compressed against wall 2: E = (1/2)(4k)y^2. Equate energies and solve (1/2)kx^2 = (1/2)(4k)y^2, giving y/x = 1/2.

On the right side, only S1 acts, so a block of mass m released from amplitude x reaches the equilibrium position with speed v = omega1 x = sqrt(k/m)x. ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A block (B) is attached to two unstretched springs S1 and S2 with spring constants $k$ and $4k$, respectively (see figure I). The other ends are attached to identical supports M1 and M2 not attached to the walls. The springs and supports have negligible mass. There is no friction anywhere. The block B is displaced towards wall 1 by a small distance $x$ (figure II) and released. The block returns and moves a maximum distance $y$ towards wall 2. Displacements $x$ and $y$ are measured with respect to the equilibrium position of the block B. What is the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$?
ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A block (B) is attached to two unstretched springs S1 and S2 with spring constants $k$ and $4k$, respectively (see figure I). The other ends are attached to identical supports M1 and M2 not attached to the walls. The springs and supports have negligible mass. There is no friction anywhere. The block B is displaced towards wall 1 by a small distance $x$ (figure II) and released. The block returns and moves a maximum distance $y$ towards wall 2. Displacements $x$ and $y$ are measured with respect to the equilibrium position of the block B. What is the ratio $\frac{y}{x}$?
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: There are two schematic diagrams in the figure. In Figure I, the left side is labeled wall 2, and the right side is labeled wall 1; block B is located in the middle, connected on the left through spring S2 to support M2, and on the right through spring S1 to support M1. In Figure II, block B is moved toward wall 1, and the displacement x relative to the original equilibrium position is marked in the figure; supports M1 and M2 are drawn as movable black supports rather than fixed on the walls. The problem statement gives that the stiffness coefficient of S1 is k, the stiffness coefficient of S2 is 4k, the masses of the springs and supports are negligible, and there is no friction.

Reasoning: According to the problem statement and the diagram, the supports are not fixed on the walls and their masses are negligible, so a free massless support cannot maintain the stretching of a spring by itself to store energy; at an endpoint position, only the spring supported by the wall side stores elastic potential energy. When block B is displaced by x toward wall 1 to the right-side turning point, the support on the S2 side can move along, S2 does not store energy, and only S1 is compressed, with energy E_right = (1/2) k x^2. The block then returns and reaches the maximum displacement y toward wall 2; the S1-side support can move along and does not store energy, and only S2 is compressed, with energy E_left = (1/2)(4k)y^2. With no friction, mechanical energy is conserved, so (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2)(4k)y^2. Simplifying gives x^2 = 4y^2, therefore y/x = 1/2.
